headline: Peanut Bunker Push Has Blues Tight to the Rocks From Beavertail to Napatree
subhead: Bass are mixed in on the blitzes at first light, scup and fluke are salvaging the slow tides, and the breachways are starting to whisper albie.
body_markdown:
The peanut bunker showed up thick around Beavertail this week, balled up tight against the rocks on the last two hours of the incoming, and where there's bait like that stacked against structure, something's going to eat it. I watched three separate blow-ups off the Jamestown side Tuesday morning — bluefish mostly, three to five pounds, absolutely shredding through the pods, with a few slot bass mixed underneath picking off the scraps that drifted down. That's the pattern right now up and down this stretch of rock: bunker pushed tight to the ledges, blues on top, bass working the bottom of the water column where the current pins the bait against the boulders.

Newport side has been the same story. Castle Hill and the rocks below Brenton Point have had bunker schools sitting in the wash on the last of the ebb, and if you're there at gray light with a white bucktail or a Deadly Dick, you can cast right into the melee. Problem is the window's short — once the sun gets up and that water warms another degree or two, the bunker scatter off the structure and slide into deeper water, and the bite goes quiet until the tide turns again. I've had my best luck fishing the hour before and the hour after low, working the seam where the current pulls off the ledge into the deeper wash.

We flagged the snapper blue push a few weeks back and said the adult class would build behind it — that's exactly what's happening. The three-to-four-pound blues chewing through those bunker schools are the fish that were snappers in the back bays a month ago. They've grown into real teeth now, and if you're fishing bunker chunks or working topwater at the breachways, expect them to show up in numbers before the bass do.

Speaking of the breachways — Charlestown, Quonochontaug, and Weekapaug are all worth a look right now, though it's more bluefish and schoolie bass than anything else at the moment. I fished the Charlestown breachway on a dropping tide last weekend and picked up bluefish steadily on a green machine trolled through the rip, with one bass around 26 inches that came off a white Slug-Go worked slow along the rock wall on the inside. No albies yet that I've seen or heard about, but the water's warm enough and the bait's right — this is usually the window where the first fish start testing the breachways before the real push shows up in September. I'd start checking Napatree and the mouth of the Pawcatuck in the next two weeks, especially on a calm morning when you can actually see fins.

Fluke have been a mixed bag. The deeper holes off Sakonnet Point — that 30 to 40 foot water off the rocks — have given up some decent fish on Gulp in white or pink glow, tipped with a strip of squid, drifted slow on the last of the outgoing. Nothing to brag about size-wise, mostly 16 to 19 inches, but enough keepers mixed in to make it worth the drift. Second Beach and the sandy stretches toward Sachuest have been slower — that warm surface water has fluke laying low, less willing to chase, so you need to bounce bottom right on their nose rather than working a fast retrieve.

Scup have been the honest bite all week. Anywhere there's structure — the rocks off Beavertail, the Jamestown Bridge pilings, the reef off Watch Hill — you can load a cooler with scup on squid strips and sandworms fished on high-low rigs in 15 to 25 feet. It's not glamorous but it's reliable, and on the days the bass and blues go quiet on you, that's where I've been filling out the trip.

Tog talk is starting around the docks even though the real bite is still weeks off. A few guys have been scouting the ledges off Watch Hill and around Napatree on green crabs during the slack tide, just checking which cracks are holding fish before the fall run gets serious. Too early to call it a pattern, but worth keeping in the back of your head as September approaches and that water starts to cool.

Looking ahead, the tide's been building toward the August 28 full moon, and that stronger flow should tighten the bunker schools even further against the rocks and sharpen up those dawn windows at Newport and Jamestown. If the wind stays cooperative — southwest and light, which is what we've had — I'd expect the blitz pattern to hold through the weekend. Watch for any shift to a hard onshore blow, though; that'll blow the bait off the ledges and scatter everything into deeper water fast. My plan for the next few days is early mornings on the Newport rocks for blues and mixed bass, then sliding down to the breachways midday to keep an eye out for that first sign of albies. It's close. Not there yet, but close.
